result: Seven subjects participated in a 14-day training study where they received real-time feedback on motor unit discharge patterns from the tibialis anterior muscle and learned to control pairs of motor units to track targets in 2D space. Overall performance improved significantly from first to last day of training (target hits: 41.19±17.76% to 67.04±18.17%, p=0.028; angle hits: 64.37±13.15% to 81.11±9.84%, p=0.016; performance metric: 0.56±0.09 to 0.69±0.10, p=0.016), with an average of 11.04±3.34 motor units reliably decomposed per subject.
evaluation: Claims C2-C4, C20, C27-C29, and C89-C95 provide comprehensive experimental details and statistically significant results demonstrating that subjects learned to control motor units with improved performance over training. The study design, subject characteristics, and quantitative outcomes with appropriate statistical tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with p<0.05) support this result.

result: Motor unit de-recruitment thresholds often differed from recruitment thresholds, with motor units continuing to discharge below their initial recruitment threshold. Recruitment and de-recruitment thresholds showed a strong correlation (R=0.53, p<0.001), with de-recruitment occurring on average 1.11±2.44% MVC below recruitment threshold in 66.7% of cases, though the overall effect was weak (p=0.111).
evaluation: Claims C21-C26 and C37 provide consistent evidence of recruitment-derecruitment hysteresis with appropriate statistical analysis. The correlation analysis (C23, C37) and descriptive statistics (C24-C25) are well-documented, though the weak overall effect (C26, p=0.111) appropriately qualifies the strength of the finding.

result: Performance improvement varied across target types, with no significant improvement for TI (p=0.938) or TII (p=0.109), but significant improvement for TIII (0.33±0.12 to 0.59±0.17, p=0.016). Within-session learning was minimal across all targets (mean correlations: TI 0.037±0.078, TII 0.066±0.094, TIII 0.043±0.074, p=0.103).
evaluation: Claims C30-C33 provide target-specific performance data with appropriate statistical tests showing differential learning across targets. The significant improvement only for TIII and minimal within-session learning are well-documented with Wilcoxon signed-rank and Friedman tests.

result: Performance in reaching different targets depended on the difference in recruitment thresholds between motor unit pairs. For TI, performance increased significantly with larger threshold differences (0.61±0.16 to 0.90±0.05, p=0.016). For TII, no dependency was detected (p=0.578). For TIII, performance decreased significantly with larger threshold differences (0.66±0.09 to 0.55±0.04, p=0.016).
evaluation: Claims C34-C36 demonstrate a clear relationship between motor unit recruitment threshold differences and task performance with appropriate statistical testing. The opposite effects for TI versus TIII are logically consistent with the task requirements and provide mechanistic insight.

result: Subjects reported feeling control over MU2 when reaching TIII (86% of cases) and described using a consistent strategy (95% of cases): rapid force increase via ankle dorsiflexion followed by slow release until cursor movement toward the vertical axis.
evaluation: Claims C38-C40 provide consistent subjective reports from questionnaire data describing the control strategy. The high percentages (86%, 95%) and specific strategy description align with the objective behavioral data, though subjective reports have inherent limitations.

result: Direct movements to targets (without activating the other motor unit) were common for TI (76-94% across conditions) but rare for TIII (1-7% across conditions). All subjects moved directly to TI in >70% of successful attempts, while only three subjects achieved direct movement to TIII in >5% of attempts. Most direct TIII movements (91.67%) occurred after trials requiring MU2 activation.
evaluation: Claims C41-C46 provide comprehensive quantitative evidence showing the asymmetry in direct movement capability between TI and TIII. The trial history effects (C45-C46) support the interpretation that TIII activation depends on prior motor unit activity rather than independent control.

result: In rare cases of direct movement to TIII, MU2 was recruited at 48.43±22.46% lower force levels than during normal ramp recruitment, with slightly lower global EMG values across all measured muscles (TA: -15.91±9.67%; FL: -18.75±23.27%; GL: -9.99±31.53%; GM: -0.02±27.31%).
evaluation: Claims C47-C48 provide quantitative comparisons of force and EMG during different recruitment conditions. The substantial reduction in force level and consistent EMG changes across muscles support altered recruitment conditions, though the small number of direct TIII movements limits generalizability.

result: Subjects used a three-stage approach to reach TIII with significantly different force levels at each stage (p<0.001). This strategy worked even when MU2 de-recruited before MU1 (24.31% of indirect TIII hits for four subjects with measured de-recruitment thresholds).
evaluation: Claims C49-C50 provide statistical evidence (Friedman test, p<0.001) for distinct force modulation stages and demonstrate the strategy's effectiveness across different motor unit de-recruitment patterns. The quantitative data support the three-stage control mechanism.

result: Pre-post experiment comparisons showed minimal changes in force (-0.18±2.33% MVC) and TA EMG (-2.35±22.62%), but slight increases in antagonist muscle EMG (FL: 5.45±28.58%; GL: 14.12±37.53%; GM: 18.41±26.51%). These changes indicate that overall recruitment order did not change critically, with antagonist increases possibly explained by fatigue.
evaluation: Claims C51-C54 provide pre-post comparisons showing minimal changes in primary outcome measures with appropriate interpretation. The small changes in force and TA EMG support the conclusion that recruitment order was preserved, though the antagonist EMG increases and fatigue explanation (C54) are speculative.

result: Validation study comparing surface and intramuscular EMG decomposition showed >94% rate of agreement in a representative case, with no errors in first or last discharges (recruitment/de-recruitment detection). Across all validation cases (16 contractions with common motor units from 36 total), agreement was >90% in all phases (ramp-up: 93.2±1.3%, constant: 92.6±1.5%, ramp-down: 95.5±2.0%), with 1ms accuracy for onset/offset detection.
evaluation: Claims C55-C63 provide comprehensive validation data demonstrating high accuracy of the online decomposition method across different contraction phases. The >90% agreement rates, perfect onset/offset detection, and consistency across multiple cases strongly support the reliability of the motor unit identification method used in the main experiment.

result: Control strategies rarely corresponded to volitional control of independent inputs to individual motor units during initial recruitment. Instead, motor unit activation was consistent with common input to the motor unit pair, with individual activation achieved predominantly through alterations in de-recruitment order explained by history-dependent changes in motor neuron excitability. Subjects did not exploit potential neural structures with selective inputs to individual motor units, and converting common input to independent input within the same task appears extremely challenging for the CNS.
evaluation: Claims C5-C9, C64-C65, C75-C78, and C86-C88 present the main conclusions consistently supported by the experimental data showing: (1) rare direct TIII movements (C41-C42), (2) trial history effects (C45-C46), (3) three-stage control strategy (C49-C50), and (4) recruitment-derecruitment hysteresis (C21-C26). The convergence of multiple lines of evidence strongly supports the conclusion that flexible motor unit control relies on common input and history-dependent mechanisms rather than independent synaptic inputs.

result: The observed recruitment-derecruitment hysteresis and variability in motor unit activation may be explained by persistent inward currents (PICs) affecting low-threshold motor units, combined with locally acting inhibition. PICs act diffusely across motor unit pools but may be focalized by local inhibition, and synaptic inhibition follows the size principle with smaller motor neurons showing greater hyperpolarization.
evaluation: Claims C66-C73 provide mechanistic interpretations based on prior literature (PICs, inhibition, size principle) to explain the experimental observations. However, these mechanisms were not directly measured in this study (acknowledged in the Discussion), making these interpretations plausible but speculative. The citation to simulation work (C73) provides some support, but direct experimental evidence is lacking.

result: Direct proof of altered motor unit recruitment due to independent input requires demonstrating activation of a higher-threshold motor unit before a lower-threshold unit during initial activation phase, without preceding activations.
evaluation: Claim C74 establishes a clear methodological criterion for demonstrating flexible motor unit control. This criterion is logically sound as it distinguishes true independent control from history-dependent effects, and is appropriately used to evaluate the experimental results.

result: Background claims establish that neural interfaces enable real-time non-invasive tracking of motor neuron activity, hundreds to thousands of motor neurons innervate muscles, motor units are typically activated in stereotyped ways following Henneman's size principle, and there is evidence for neural substrates allowing selective cortical control of motor units.
evaluation: Claims C1, C11-C19 present established knowledge from the field supported by appropriate citations. These background claims provide context for the study but are not novel findings. The citations to prior work (Henneman 1957, Heckman & Enoka 2012, Marshall et al. 2021, etc.) support these statements.

result: Prior work shows subjects can learn motor unit control with biofeedback, variations in force direction and motor behavior can impact recruitment order, and motor unit pool synergies exist similar to muscle synergies. The tibialis anterior was selected for its favorable properties for surface EMG decomposition and monosynaptic cortical connections.
evaluation: Claims C79-C85 provide relevant background from prior literature with appropriate citations and justify the experimental design choices (muscle selection). These claims contextualize the current work but are not novel findings from this study.

result: High-density surface EMG was acquired from tibialis anterior using a 64-electrode grid, sampled at 2048 Hz, with the foot locked to allow only ankle dorsiflexion.
evaluation: Claims C96-C98 describe the data acquisition methods with specific technical details. These methodological details are clearly stated and appropriate for the experimental design, supporting reproducibility.
